items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "foreshadowing".
items.answer: Hints or clues about what will happen later in a story
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: hints or clues about what will happen later in a story. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "Suspense means lots of action and violence." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Suspense comes from uncertainty and anticipation; quiet details such as a warm door handle can be more suspenseful than action.
items.markingKey: Suspense comes from uncertainty and anticipation; quiet details such as a warm door handle can be more suspenseful than action. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

Analyse how pacing is used to create tension in the extract.
items.answer: Suspense is built through a mystery (a light under a locked door), a rhetorical question, slow pacing with short sentences on the stairs, unsettling sensory details (creaking steps, a warm handle) and a final revelation that creates a cliffhanger.
items.markingKey: Suspense is built through a mystery (a light under a locked door), a rhetorical question, slow pacing with short sentences on the stairs, unsettling sensory details (creaking steps, a warm handle) and a final revelation that creates a cliffhanger. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence to build more suspense: "Ravi opened the door and saw a figure."
items.answer: For example: "Ravi's fingers closed round the handle. Cold. He pushed. The door groaned. In the darkness, something moved." Credit short sentences, sensory detail and delay.
items.markingKey: For example: "Ravi's fingers closed round the handle. Cold. He pushed. The door groaned. In the darkness, something moved." Credit short sentences, sensory detail and delay.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in a tower block in Hong Kong.

The lift stopped between the 23rd and 24th floors with a soft clunk.
The lights dimmed to emergency orange. Kenji pressed the alarm. Nothing.
'Don't worry,' said the old woman in the corner. 'It happens every Tuesday.'
It was Wednesday.
Kenji looked at her properly for the first time. Her umbrella was dripping, though it hadn't rained all week. And in the mirrored wall, where her reflection should have been, there was only an umbrella, dripping, all by itself.

Analyse how the phrase "It was Wednesday." helps the writer achieve their purpose.
items.answer: One-line paragraph: "It was Wednesday." – the short paragraph undercuts the woman's reassurance and signals that something is wrong.
items.markingKey: One-line paragraph: "It was Wednesday." – the short paragraph undercuts the woman's reassurance and signals that something is wrong. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story with a twist ending.

Every night that week, Sam heard footsteps following her home from the bus stop. Every night she walked faster. Every night she didn't look back.
On Friday she couldn't bear it. At the corner she spun round, fists raised.
A small boy in a yellow raincoat stopped dead. He was holding out her purse.
'You dropped it on Monday,' he whispered. 'I've been trying to catch up.'

Explain how the twist in the final line contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The twist in the final line: it reveals the innocent truth and makes the reader rethink the whole story.
items.markingKey: The twist in the final line: it reveals the innocent truth and makes the reader rethink the whole story. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:

She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

How does the writer build suspense in this extract?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The writer builds suspense through mystery and pacing. The rhetorical question "So why, tonight, was there a light under it?" draws the reader in; the simile "Each creak sounded like a warning" makes ordinary sounds threatening; short sentences ("It was warm.") slow the climb and focus on unsettling details; and the final isolated sentence about Leila's mother creates a shocking cliffhanger.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The writer builds suspense through mystery and pacing. The rhetorical question "So why, tonight, was there a light under it?" draws the reader in; the simile "Each creak sounded like a warning" makes ordinary sounds threatening; short sentences ("It was warm.") slow the climb and focus on unsettling details; and the final isolated sentence about Leila's mother creates a shocking cliffhanger. items.stem: Analyse how the writer of a suspense story you have read uses pacing and foreshadowing to keep the reader in suspense.

items.stem: Briefly explain why withholding information builds suspense.
items.answer: When readers do not know what is behind the door or who is following, they keep reading to find out.

items.stem: Distinguish between suspense and surprise.
items.answer: Suspense is a lasting feeling of anxious expectation built over time; surprise is a sudden, unexpected moment. A twist ending gives surprise after a build-up of suspense.
items.markingKey: Suspense is a lasting feeling of anxious expectation built over time; surprise is a sudden, unexpected moment. A twist ending gives surprise after a build-up of suspense. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story with a twist ending.

Analyse how pacing is used to create tension in the extract.
items.answer: Suspense builds through repetition ("Every night..."), Sam's fear and her refusal to look back; the turning point on Friday raises the tension to a climax.

items.stem: "A suspense story must end with a twist." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Twists can be effective if well foreshadowed, but suspense can also end with an open or quiet resolution; the ending should fit the story.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: twists surprise and satisfy readers; they make readers rethink the story. Arguments against: a predictable twist can disappoint; open endings or realistic resolutions can also be powerful. Supported judgement: Twists can be effective if well foreshadowed, but suspense can also end with an open or quiet resolution; the ending should fit the story. items.stem: "The lights dimmed to emergency orange." Which sense does this appeal to?
items.answer: Sight

items.stem: Distinguish between setting and atmosphere.
items.answer: Setting is where and when a story takes place; atmosphere is the feeling the description of that setting creates for the reader.
items.markingKey: Setting is where and when a story takes place; atmosphere is the feeling the description of that setting creates for the reader. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Setting is just background information." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Setting creates atmosphere, reflects characters' feelings and can drive the plot (a stuck lift, a storm).
items.markingKey: Setting creates atmosphere, reflects characters' feelings and can drive the plot (a stuck lift, a storm). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write two sentences describing an abandoned railway station at night, using at least two senses.
items.answer: Any vivid description using two senses (e.g. sound of dripping water, smell of rust). 1 mark each sense, 1 for atmosphere.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Description of setting slows a story down too much."
items.answer: Overlong description can slow a story, but precise sensory details build the atmosphere that suspense depends on.

items.stem: Explain why "it was all a dream" is often a weak twist.
items.answer: It cancels the story's events and stakes, making the reader feel cheated rather than surprised.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It cancels the story's events and stakes, making the reader feel cheated rather than surprised. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

Comment on the writer's choice of language in "Her mother had been gone for six years.".
items.answer: Cliffhanger: "Her mother had been gone for six years." – the final revelation shocks the reader and leaves the mystery unresolved.
items.markingKey: Cliffhanger: "Her mother had been gone for six years." – the final revelation shocks the reader and leaves the mystery unresolved. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain the difference between setting and atmosphere.
items.answer: Setting is where and when a story takes place; atmosphere is the feeling the description of that setting creates for the reader.
items.markingKey: Setting is where and when a story takes place; atmosphere is the feeling the description of that setting creates for the reader. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the climax and the resolution.
items.answer: The climax is the moment of greatest tension (spinning round to face the follower); the resolution reveals the outcome (it is a boy with her purse).
items.markingKey: The climax is the moment of greatest tension (spinning round to face the follower); the resolution reveals the outcome (it is a boy with her purse). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why writers use short sentences at moments of tension.
items.answer: Short sentences slow the reader down, focus on each detail and mimic a character's quickened heartbeat, increasing suspense.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Short sentences slow the reader down, focus on each detail and mimic a character's quickened heartbeat, increasing suspense. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: an elderly woman and a teenage girl sit on a train platform in Mumbai, sharing earphones; the departures board shows "DELAYED".]

Write a descriptive paragraph (about 150 words) that recreates this scene using at least three senses.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a warm, quiet and bittersweet mood; possible idea – a grandmother and granddaughter on their last journey together, a delayed train that changes a decision, or music that bridges generations; techniques such as dialogue to reveal character, a symbol (the shared earphones), a flashback; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a warm, quiet and bittersweet mood; possible idea – a grandmother and granddaughter on their last journey together, a delayed train that changes a decision, or music that bridges generations; techniques such as dialogue to reveal character, a symbol (the shared earphones), a flashback; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: "A good twist should have no clues so that nobody can guess it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Fair clues are needed so the twist makes sense; the skill is hiding them in plain sight.
items.markingKey: Fair clues are needed so the twist makes sense; the skill is hiding them in plain sight. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Analyse the effect of the ambiguous ending in the text.
items.answer: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives.
items.markingKey: The ambiguous ending: we do not learn whether Thabo takes the reward; his gentle words suggest kindness comes first, leaving the reader to judge his motives. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a mountain village in Nepal after an earthquake; a girl carries a school whiteboard on her back up a dusty path.]

Write the opening paragraph (about 150 words) of a story inspired by this image. Hook the reader and establish the mood.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a determined and hopeful mood; possible idea – rebuilding a school, a teacher's journey, or a community that refuses to give up; techniques such as contrast between destruction and hope, the rule of three, a call to action; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a determined and hopeful mood; possible idea – rebuilding a school, a teacher's journey, or a community that refuses to give up; techniques such as contrast between destruction and hope, the rule of three, a call to action; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: two hands, one old and one young, holding the same chess piece above a board in a park in Moscow.]
Image 2: [A photograph: a cracked smartphone screen lit up in the dark, showing 47 unread messages.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a crowd of students marching with hand-painted placards that read "THERE IS NO PLANET B"; one younger girl is on her father's shoulders.]

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques: symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the game begins – memories surface – the final move; techniques: symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "A suspense story must end with a twist."
items.answer: Twists can be effective if well foreshadowed, but suspense can also end with an open or quiet resolution; the ending should fit the story.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: twists surprise and satisfy readers; they make readers rethink the story. Arguments against: a predictable twist can disappoint; open endings or realistic resolutions can also be powerful. Supported judgement: Twists can be effective if well foreshadowed, but suspense can also end with an open or quiet resolution; the ending should fit the story.

items.stem: "Description of setting slows a story down too much." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Overlong description can slow a story, but precise sensory details build the atmosphere that suspense depends on.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: readers may skip long description; action keeps pace. Arguments against: setting creates mood that makes events frightening; well-chosen details can be brief. Supported judgement: Overlong description can slow a story, but precise sensory details build the atmosphere that suspense depends on. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

Write the next paragraph (about 200 words): what does Leila find when she opens the door? Keep the suspense and include a twist.
items.answer: Indicative content: consistent setting and mood; slow pacing at the moment of opening; sensory detail; a twist that links to the mother (e.g. a recording, a sibling, a memory) rather than a cliché; a final line that resolves or deepens the mystery.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: consistent setting and mood; slow pacing at the moment of opening; sensory detail; a twist that links to the mother (e.g. a recording, a sibling, a memory) rather than a cliché; a final line that resolves or deepens the mystery. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).
